lecture11.title: Masses and Springs · Theory and Prediction

sections.title: Masses and Springs · Theory and Prediction
One mass, two directions
teaching: An **oscillation** is repeated motion around an **equilibrium position**, the position where the mass can rest. A spring that is stretched or squeezed acts to bring the mass back toward equilibrium. The moving mass has **inertia**, which means that it tends to keep moving. When it reaches equilibrium, it therefore continues past that position instead of stopping immediately.

Moving past equilibrium displaces the spring in the other direction. The spring's **restoring force** now acts back toward equilibrium from that side. The mass returns, passes through equilibrium again and repeats the motion. The spring provides the return toward the resting position, while the mass's tendency to keep moving carries it beyond that position.

In **longitudinal motion**, the mass moves along the spring. Its movement stretches or compresses the spring along that same line. In **transverse motion**, the mass moves across the spring line while the outer ends remain fixed. The two segments are already under **tension**, meaning they are being pulled tight. When the mass moves above or below the resting line, their pulls have components that bring it back toward the line.

The direction of movement differs, but the two examples have the same **frequency**. Frequency describes how many complete cycles occur in a given time. Here the masses and their total restoring stiffness are matched, so both motions repeat at the same rate. The examples are ideal motions without damping, so they continue instead of gradually dying away.

sections.title: Mass and stiffness change the rate
teaching: **Mass** and **stiffness** affect different parts of the motion. Mass determines how difficult it is to change how an object is moving. Stiffness determines how strongly the system acts to restore a mass that has moved away from equilibrium. Comparing systems that change one property while keeping the other unchanged shows how each property affects the rate of oscillation.

A **larger mass oscillates more slowly** when stiffness stays the same. The spring has more inertia to overcome, so it takes longer to change the mass's motion and complete a cycle. In the larger-mass row, both the longitudinal and transverse examples complete fewer cycles in the same time than their reference systems. The motion remains back and forth, but its frequency is lower.

A **stiffer system oscillates faster** when mass stays the same. The same displacement produces a stronger restoring force, so the mass's motion changes more quickly. The stiffer-system row therefore completes more cycles in the same time than the reference row. Increasing mass and increasing stiffness have opposite effects on frequency.

For these comparisons, **effective restoring stiffness** means the stiffness that brings the mass back in its actual direction of motion. In the transverse examples, this restoring action depends on the tension and arrangement of the segments. Making a spring harder to stretch along its length is not automatically the same change as increasing its return force across the spring line. The two directions have matching frequencies within each row because their masses and effective restoring stiffness are matched.

sections.title: Two masses have two normal modes
teaching: When two masses are connected, moving one can affect the other through the middle connection. With equal masses, equal connections and both outer ends fixed, there are two **normal modes**. A normal mode is a coordinated pattern in which the masses keep the same relationship to one another while oscillating at a particular frequency.

In **Mode 1**, the masses move together. Both are displaced in the same direction at the same time and reverse together. This is the lower-frequency pattern. In **Mode 2**, they move against one another. When one is displaced to one side of its resting position, the other is displaced to the opposite side. Their opposing movement disturbs the middle connection more strongly and produces a stronger restoring action, so Mode 2 is faster.

Both modes can occur in the **same two masses at once**. Each mass's position then depends on the displacement contributed by Mode 1 and the displacement contributed by Mode 2 at that moment. Contributions in the same direction add together. Contributions in opposite directions partly cancel. Adding the effects of the individual modes is called **superposition**.

The combined movement contains **both frequencies**. It looks more complicated because the two contributions change at different rates, but they remain the same two modes. The longitudinal and transverse examples show these same relationships with different directions of movement. Mode 2 has a higher frequency than Mode 1, without being exactly twice as fast.

sections.title: Pop quiz
Three masses have three normal modes
teaching: Three equal masses connected between fixed ends have **three independent normal modes**. Each mode describes how all three masses move together as a system. The mode number identifies a different coordinated pattern, rather than a different physical mass or a different direction of movement.

In **Mode 1**, all three masses move in the same direction together. The middle mass moves farther from equilibrium, while the two outer masses move equal, smaller distances. Moving together therefore means sharing the direction and timing of the motion. It does not require every mass to move the same distance. This is the lowest-frequency mode.

In **Mode 2**, the two outer masses move in opposite directions and the middle mass stays at equilibrium. In this pattern, the effects of the outer masses on the middle mass balance. The system can therefore vibrate even though one of its masses remains still. This mode has a frequency between those of Mode 1 and Mode 3.

In **Mode 3**, the outer masses move together while the middle mass moves against them. The connections between the middle and outer masses are disturbed by this opposition, producing the highest-frequency pattern. Having three modes does not mean that their frequencies are one, two and three times the lowest frequency. These discrete mass systems do not have that simple whole-number spacing.

The three modes can also contribute to **one combined motion**. Each mass's displacement is found by adding its contributions from the three patterns. The middle mass stays still in pure Mode 2, but it moves when Mode 1 or Mode 3 also contributes. A mass that is stationary in one mode is therefore still able to move in a different mode or in a mixture.

sections.title: One more mass, one more mode
teaching: Each moving mass adds another independent way for the chain to vibrate in the direction being considered. There is **one normal mode per moving mass**. The rows contain one through six masses, so they contain one through six modes respectively. The empty spaces beside the smaller systems reflect modes those systems do not have.

Within a row, the masses and connections stay the same and both endpoints remain fixed. **Mode 1** has all the masses moving together. Higher mode numbers introduce more **reversals across the chain**, with some regions displaced one way while other regions are displaced the other way. As the motion continues, those regions reverse while keeping the relationship that defines the mode.

More reversals in the same chain go with a **higher vibration frequency**. Neighboring parts increasingly oppose one another, so the connections provide a stronger restoring pattern. The change across a row therefore comes from how the masses move in relation to one another. It does not require replacing the masses or connections with different ones.

The **number of modes** does not tell us that their frequencies will be equally spaced. The discrete chains generally have frequencies that are not whole-number multiples of the lowest one. Their greatest displayed displacements are matched so the patterns can be compared directly. Colors identify the mode number in this collection, while each row identifies how many masses the system contains.

sections.title: A fixed–fixed string combines harmonics
teaching: A string fixed at both ends must stay still at those endpoints. A point with no displacement is called a **node**. **Mode 1** fits one half-wave between the ends, so the string moves back and forth with one broad region between its fixed nodes. **Modes 2, 3, 4 and 5** fit two, three, four and five half-waves into the same length. Each pattern satisfies the requirement that both ends stay still.

The frequency of Mode 1 is the **fundamental frequency**, the lowest frequency in this set. The higher modes are **consecutive harmonics**, meaning whole-number multiples of the fundamental. Both odd and even multiples are present. Fitting more half-waves into the same length gives a shorter spatial pattern and a faster oscillation. All the motions are slowed equally in the animation so these differences can be followed.

The **same string can contain several modes at once**. Its actual displacement at each point is the sum of the displacements contributed by the modes. Some contributions reinforce one another and others oppose one another. The resulting shape changes over time because the individual modes pass through their cycles at different rates. A complicated shape can therefore come from combining simpler coordinated patterns.

The marked **pickup point** is where the combined motion is measured. Its **spectrum** shows which frequencies are present, with frequency in hertz along the horizontal axis and amplitude up the vertical axis. The five peaks correspond to the five modes in the mixture. Their equal heights result from the chosen amounts of each mode at that measurement point. Equal peak heights are a property of this example, rather than a requirement for every vibrating string.

sections.title: A membrane combines spatial modes
teaching: A **membrane** vibrates across a surface rather than only along a line. All four edges of this rectangular membrane remain fixed while the interior moves above and below its resting surface. A pattern can divide the surface in either of its two directions. Its mode label therefore uses two numbers to identify the divisions.

**Mode 1, labelled (1,1)**, has one broad moving region. **Mode 2, labelled (2,1)**, divides the surface in the first direction. **Mode 3, labelled (1,2)**, divides it in the other direction. **Mode 4, labelled (2,2)**, divides it in both directions, and **Mode 5, labelled (3,1)**, gives three regions along the first direction. Adjacent regions move to opposite sides of the resting surface, with stationary divisions between them. The labels describe different shapes of movement across the same surface.

The combined surface adds the five movements at every point. The marked **pickup point** identifies where that combined motion is measured. In the spectrum, frequency increases along the horizontal axis and relative amplitude increases up the vertical axis. The five peaks identify the five frequency components in the measured mixture. Their equal heights come from the chosen amount of each mode at the pickup. The combined surface is drawn with less vertical enlargement so its motion fits in its panel.

The evenly spaced **harmonic frequencies are assigned for this illustration**. They are not the natural frequencies calculated for this rectangular membrane. The example shows how surface patterns can be combined and how their frequencies can appear in a spectrum. It does not establish that natural membrane modes always form an evenly spaced harmonic series.

sections.title: Theory makes a measurable prediction
teaching: A **scientific theory** describes how a system works clearly enough to make a prediction. The prediction states what should happen when that system is measured. Differential equations provide a precise way of describing change, and their consequences can be compared with measurements. The purpose is to connect an explanation of the system to something observable.

The proposed theory treats the **vocal folds as a vibrating membrane**. Its prediction is that a measured laryngeal vibration signal will contain **equidistant harmonics**. Equidistant means that the peaks are separated by equal frequency intervals. The prediction therefore specifies a pattern to look for in the spectrum.

To test it, the experiment would measure **laryngeal vibration** and examine its spectrum. The comparison concerns the spacing between the frequency peaks. Evenly spaced peaks would agree with the stated prediction. A different pattern would raise a question about whether the proposed model accounts for that signal.

The material proposes this experiment without supplying a measured outcome. The membrane animation uses assigned harmonic frequencies, so that illustration alone does not show that a natural membrane must have the same spacing. Testing the vocal-fold prediction requires an actual vibration measurement and a comparison with the predicted spectrum.

sections.title: One fixed end and one free end
teaching: A string with **one fixed end and one free end** has different requirements at its two boundaries. The fixed bottom cannot move, so it is a **displacement node**. The free top moves and is a **displacement antinode**, a point where the mode reaches its greatest displacement. An allowed pattern must have a node at the bottom and an antinode at the top at the same time.

**Mode 1** fits a quarter-wavelength between those endpoints. The shape begins at a stationary point and reaches a moving maximum at the free end. **Modes 2, 3 and 4** fit three, five and seven quarter-wavelengths. Adding a full half-wave allows a more complex pattern while preserving the fixed bottom and free top.

These modes have the **odd harmonics**, the fundamental followed by its third, fifth and seventh multiples. An even number of quarter-wavelengths would put a node at the top. That would make the top stationary, which does not match the free-end condition. The missing even harmonics therefore follow from the kinds of movement allowed at the two endpoints.

The spectrum shows frequency in hertz along the horizontal axis and amplitude up the vertical axis. Its four equal-height peaks represent **equal excitation of the four modes** when their mixture is measured at the free end. Each mode has an antinode there, so each can contribute to the measurement. The animation slows all the motions equally to make their shapes and different rates visible.

The fixed–fixed and fixed–free demonstrations are **separately tuned** to have a matching fundamental frequency. Changing only a fixed end to a free end, while keeping length and wave speed the same, would halve the fundamental. Giving both examples the same fundamental therefore also requires a change of length or wave speed.

sections.title: Masses and Springs in Speech Production
Dynamic systems in economic stabilization
teaching: A system can change over time as its parts influence one another. In an economy, those changes can include boom-and-bust cycles. Woodford’s **Dynamic Stochastic General Equilibrium**, or DSGE, is the theory named in the economic example. It concerns changing economic behavior, making economics another setting in which a theory of a system can be used to understand fluctuations.

**Stabilization** means reducing the size of peaks and troughs. Unemployment is represented by the black line and inflation by the gray line. Their large, jagged changes become smaller and smoother in the stabilization illustration. The aim is to avoid harmful extremes such as high unemployment or runaway inflation. The shared question across these changing systems is what produces a fluctuation and what change could reduce it.

sections.title: One mass, two directions
teaching: A mass attached to a spring can move back and forth because the mass and the spring contribute different parts of the behavior. The spring pushes or pulls toward **equilibrium**, the resting position. A moving mass has **inertia**, which means it tends to keep moving. When the mass reaches equilibrium, it continues past it, stretches or compresses the spring the other way, and is then pushed or pulled back again. This repeated back-and-forth movement is an oscillation.

In longitudinal movement, the mass travels along the spring. In transverse movement, the mass travels across the line between the supports. The transverse springs are already under tension. Moving the mass away from that line changes the direction of their pull, so part of the force pulls it back toward the line.

Both movements can repeat at the same rate when the moving mass and the total restoring stiffness match. **Frequency** describes how often a complete back-and-forth cycle repeats. Direction alone does not set that frequency. These examples use an ideal system without damping, so the oscillations continue. The transverse model describes small movements around an already tensioned resting state, with the visible movement enlarged so that it can be followed.

sections.title: Mass and stiffness change the rate
teaching: A greater **mass** is harder to speed up, slow down, or turn around. If the spring’s restoring stiffness stays the same, the heavier mass changes its motion more slowly. Each back-and-forth cycle takes longer, so the frequency falls. The larger mass therefore completes fewer cycles than the reference mass in the same amount of time.

Greater **stiffness** means a stronger restoring force for the same movement away from equilibrium. If the mass stays the same, a stiffer system changes the motion more quickly and completes each cycle sooner. The frequency rises. Keeping one property unchanged while changing the other separates the slowing effect of mass from the speeding effect of stiffness.

The same reasoning applies to movement along the spring and across the spring line when their effective restoring stiffnesses match. Effective stiffness means the restoring effect in the direction the mass actually moves. In the transverse case, that effect depends on tension and the arrangement of the springs. Making an axial spring stiffer while leaving its tension unchanged is not automatically the same change. The comparisons use ideal motion without friction or damping.

sections.title: Two masses have two normal modes
teaching: Two equal masses connected by three equal spring-like links between fixed ends can move in two coordinated patterns. A **normal mode** is a pattern in which the parts maintain a particular relationship while the whole pattern repeats at one frequency. With two movable masses, there are two independent modes in the direction being considered. The colors identify the individual masses, and the dashed marks identify their resting positions.

In **Mode 1**, both masses move in the same direction together. Their separation changes little, so the middle spring changes relatively little. This pattern has the lower frequency. In Mode 2, the masses move in opposite directions. They move toward one another and then away from one another, making the middle spring compress and stretch more strongly. More of the restoring action is involved, so this pattern repeats faster.

These relationships occur both when the masses move along the spring line and when they move across it, provided that the effective spring connections match. A chain made of separate masses has its own allowed frequencies. Having two modes does not mean that the second frequency must be exactly twice the first.

The two modes can also contribute at the same time. Their movements are added at each mass at each instant. Contributions in the same direction make a larger movement, while contributions in opposite directions partly cancel. This is **superposition**. The resulting movement contains both original frequencies rather than becoming a third normal mode with one new frequency. The combined movement is drawn at a reduced size so that the masses remain distinct.

sections.title: Three masses have three normal modes
teaching: Adding a third movable mass gives the connected system three independent **normal modes**. The three equal masses are connected by four equal spring-like links between fixed ends. The colors keep the identities of the masses clear as they move. The coordinated patterns occur in both the longitudinal and transverse versions when their effective connections match.

In Mode 1, all three masses move to the same side of equilibrium together. The middle mass moves farthest, and the outer two move equal, smaller distances. This broad movement has the lowest frequency. In Mode 2, the outer masses move in opposite directions while the middle mass stays at equilibrium. The pulls on the middle balance in this pattern. Its motionless location is a **node**, meaning that its displacement stays zero throughout that mode’s cycle.

In Mode 3, the outer masses move together and the middle mass moves against them. Neighboring masses therefore move differently in more places along the chain. The connections between them undergo more relative change, and the restoring action makes this the fastest pattern. The three frequencies belong to this particular chain; they are not an exact sequence of one, two, and three times the lowest frequency.

When all three modes are added, each mass follows their combined contributions. The middle mass now moves because Modes 1 and 3 both contribute movement there. Being a node in Mode 2 does not make it a permanently fixed point. Its behavior depends on which modes are active.

sections.title: One more mass, one more mode
teaching: Each additional movable mass gives the connected chain another independent way to move. One mass has one mode, two masses have two, and this relationship continues through the six-mass chain with six modes. This count concerns movement in the displayed direction. The endpoints remain fixed, and the masses and spring connections are equal within the chains.

Within one chain, the lowest mode has the broadest pattern. Neighboring masses move together. Higher modes introduce more reversals, with different groups moving in opposite directions and small-motion locations between them. The connections must stretch or change direction more strongly, and the higher patterns repeat faster. Colors identify the mode number here, rather than the identity of one mass.

A chain cannot have more independent modes than movable masses in the direction being modeled. The empty part of the arrangement therefore corresponds to modes that those smaller chains do not have. All the available patterns are represented, making 21 comparisons across the six chains.

The largest visible movement has been scaled to match across the panels. **Amplitude**, the size of the movement away from the resting position, is different from frequency, the rate of repetition. A taller movement is not necessarily a faster one. These chains of separate masses also generally have frequencies that are not exact whole-number multiples of their lowest frequency. Mode count and harmonic spacing are different properties.

sections.title: A fixed–fixed string combines harmonics
teaching: An ideal continuous string fixed at both ends has to stay still at both supports. Each fixed endpoint is a **node**. The simplest standing pattern fits one half-wave into the string’s length, forming one broad moving arch. The next fits two half-waves and has a node in the middle. Further patterns fit three, four, and five half-waves, with more internal nodes and more regions moving in opposite directions.

Fitting a greater number of half-waves into the same length produces a pattern that repeats faster when the string’s wave speed stays the same. These allowed frequencies are **harmonics**, or whole-number multiples of the lowest frequency. Both odd and even multiples occur because either an odd or an even number of half-waves can end at two fixed nodes. This exact relationship belongs to the ideal continuous-string model.

All five patterns can contribute to one string at once. At each position, their displacements are added to give the string’s actual position. Some contributions reinforce one another while others cancel, so the overall outline changes in a complicated way even though its component motions are regular. The movement is slowed by the same amount for all modes, preserving their relative rates.

A pickup at the marked point measures the movement at that location. A **spectrum** separates the recorded movement into its frequency components. Frequency is on the horizontal axis, and peak height represents amplitude. The five peaks are equal because the component strengths were chosen to give equal contributions at this pickup. Equal heights depend on the particular strengths and measurement position.

sections.title: Mass, stiffness, position, and frequency
teaching: Mass and stiffness influence frequency through different physical roles. A greater moving mass responds more slowly to a given restoring force, so it lowers frequency when stiffness stays the same. A stiffer system supplies a stronger restoring force for the same displacement, so it raises frequency when mass stays the same.

The effect of changing one small region also depends on how that region behaves in the mode. Added mass matters most where the material moves strongly back and forth. At a node, there is little or no movement for the added mass to take part in. The same added mass can therefore strongly slow one mode but have little effect on another mode that hardly moves there.

**Movement and stretching** are different. Neighbors can travel together while keeping nearly the same distance between them. There is then substantial movement but little local stretching or compression. Where neighbors move differently, their separation changes strongly. A region can therefore have strong stretching or compression near a point whose own movement is small. Increasing stiffness matters most where that changing separation is important. In the ideal standing patterns, the places with greatest movement alternate with the places with greatest local stretching or compression.

The allowed patterns also depend on the system’s ends. A chain of separate masses has one independent mode per movable mass in the modeled direction, generally without exact whole-number frequency spacing. An ideal continuous string fixed at both ends fits whole numbers of half-waves and has whole-number harmonics. A fixed–free system fits odd numbers of quarter-waves and has odd-multiple resonances. Identifying the system and its movement pattern gives the basis for predicting a frequency change.

sections.title: A fixed–fixed string combines harmonics
teaching: A string’s different modes can be active at the same time. Each mode contributes a movement at every position, and the contributions add to give one actual string shape. Because the ends are fixed, each contribution stays zero there. Higher modes add more internal nodes and more alternating moving regions along the string.

The combined shape changes as the contributions move through their cycles. Where two contributions point the same way, they reinforce one another. Where they point opposite ways, they partly cancel. A part of the string can briefly look almost flat because of cancellation and then become displaced as the contributions change. The mixture still contains all five mode frequencies.

A **pickup** records the movement at one marked point. It does not record the entire outline of the string. The spectrum of that changing signal identifies its component frequencies horizontally and their amplitudes by peak height. The ideal fixed–fixed string has whole-number harmonics, with higher modes completing more cycles in the same time. The specially chosen mode strengths make the five measured peaks equal at this pickup; other points can receive different-sized contributions from the same modes.

sections.title: A local change affects two modes differently
teaching: The small highlighted region is left of the string’s midpoint. In Mode 4, it lies in a broad moving region where neighboring positions move by similar amounts. There is substantial back-and-forth movement but relatively little local stretching. In Mode 5, it lies near a small-motion point where neighboring positions change more strongly relative to one another. There is more local stretching.

Adding mass in that region strongly affects Mode 4 because the added mass takes part in its substantial movement. More inertia makes that mode slower and lowers its frequency. Mode 5 moves much less in the same region, so adding the same mass has little effect on its frequency. This comparison concerns how far the material moves over a cycle, rather than whether one frozen frame catches it momentarily at rest.

Increasing stiffness there has the opposite pattern of importance. It adds little restoring action to Mode 4 because there is little local stretching. It adds more restoring action to Mode 5 because that mode stretches the region strongly. Mode 5’s frequency therefore rises. If mass and stiffness both increase in the marked region, the dominant effects are **Mode 4 lower and Mode 5 higher**. The outcome depends on what each mode does at that location.

sections.title: A membrane combines spatial modes
teaching: A **membrane** is a surface that can move in two directions across its area, while moving above and below its resting plane. Its edges stay fixed in this model. Because patterns can divide the surface along either direction, two numbers identify each pattern. They count the moving regions along the two directions.

The pattern labeled (1,1) has one broad moving region. The (2,1) pattern has two opposing regions along the first direction, and (1,2) has two along the other. The (2,2) pattern divides in both directions, producing four regions. The (3,1) pattern has three moving regions along the first direction. These are different coordinated movements of one surface.

When all five modes contribute, their displacements add at every position. Their movements can reinforce or cancel as the cycles progress. The combined surface is displayed at a reduced vertical scale so that it fits in its panel. Its apparent height therefore cannot be compared directly with the individual panels’ heights.

The marked pickup measures movement at one point, and the spectrum identifies the frequencies and their relative amplitudes there. The equally spaced frequencies were assigned to make an illustrative harmonic series, and the mode strengths were selected to make the measured peaks equal. They are not the natural frequencies calculated for this rectangle. The combined movement and its spectrum explain how several surface patterns can be present together, with the displayed spacing coming from the assigned frequencies.

sections.title: Theory makes a measurable prediction
teaching: A **theory** states relationships clearly enough to predict what a system will do. For a changing physical system, differential equations describe how quantities change and how they affect one another. Working out the behavior predicted by those relationships gives an observation to look for in an experiment. The measurement can then be compared with the prediction.

The proposed vocal-fold model treats the folds as a vibrating membrane and predicts regularly spaced **harmonic peaks** in a laryngeal vibration signal. Testing that prediction requires recording actual laryngeal vibration and examining the signal’s spectrum. The relevant result would be the spacing of its frequency components, not simply whether the vocal folds move.

The membrane animation’s frequencies were assigned. An independently recorded signal supplies a separate test of the proposed harmonic spacing. The material gives the prediction and the experiment to perform, but it supplies no measured experimental outcome.

sections.title: One fixed end and one free end
teaching: A fixed endpoint must stay still, so it is a **node**. A free endpoint can move strongly and forms an antinode, a place with maximum movement in the mode. With a fixed bottom and a free top, an allowed pattern must meet both conditions. The simplest pattern fits a quarter-wave between the two ends.

Adding a half-wave preserves the same two endpoint conditions. The next patterns therefore fit three, five, and seven quarter-waves. Their frequencies are **odd multiples** of the lowest frequency. An even number of quarter-waves would finish with the wrong condition at the free end. Which patterns fit is determined by what each end is allowed to do.

The spectrum puts frequency along the horizontal axis and amplitude vertically. The four-mode mixture has equal peaks when the modes are equally excited and measured at the free end, where all four have strong movement. The visible movement is slowed equally across the modes, preserving the difference in their rates.

The fixed–fixed and fixed–free examples have been separately tuned to have the same lowest frequency. If only the endpoint were released while length and wave speed stayed unchanged, the lowest frequency would fall by half. The simplest pattern would fit a quarter-wave instead of a half-wave. Keeping the same lowest frequency across the two examples therefore requires retuning length or wave speed as well.

sections.title: Air in a fixed–free tube has modes
teaching: Air can be modeled as small masses joined by spring-like connections. The masses represent **inertia**, the tendency of moving air to keep moving. The connections represent the restoring effect that occurs when air is compressed. This simplified vocal-tract tube is treated as fixed at the glottis and free at the open lips.

The air elements move **longitudinally**, back and forth along the tube. Mode 1 is the lowest coordinated pattern and is F1-like. Mode 2 is the next pattern and is F2-like. F1 and F2 name the first and second formants, which are resonances of the air system. The first pattern has broad movement, while the second includes an additional reversal along the tube. In the uniform reference, Mode 2 repeats three times as fast as Mode 1, following the fixed–free odd-multiple relationship.

The locations are measured from the glottis toward the lips. The /a/ region is about one-third of the way along, the /i/ region about two-thirds, and /u/ acts near the lips. Each marked location lies in both mode patterns, but its role can differ between them. Strong movement at one location makes a mass change influential, while strong compression makes a change in springiness influential. A constriction’s location can therefore change how it affects F1 and F2.

sections.title: Vowel shape locates a constriction
teaching: A **constriction** is a place where the air passage narrows. Changing the tongue and lips changes where that narrowing occurs. The MRI examples organize tongue positions by height and by front–back location. “dean” is high and front, “Dan” is low and front, “dune” is high and back, “Don” is low and back, and “done” is central.

The high-front “dean” example has its labeled constriction about two-thirds of the distance from the glottis toward the lips. The “dune” example has a constriction at the lips. The low-back “Don” example has a constriction about one-third of the distance from the glottis. The central “done” reference is labeled “No constriction.” These positions describe where the air passage changes along its length.

A narrowing changes the local effective mass and springiness of the air model. Effective mass describes the inertia involved in the movement, while springiness describes the restoring effect involved in compression. How much either change influences a mode depends on what the air does in that region. The tongue’s height and front–back position describe articulation; the location within each movement pattern explains the consequences for its resonance.

sections.title: Blank source page
Air in a fixed–free tube has modes
teaching: The two air modes occupy one simplified tube, fixed at the glottal end and free at the lips. Mode 1 is F1-like, and Mode 2 is F2-like. The second pattern has more internal changes in movement direction and repeats faster. In the uniform reference, it repeats three times as fast as the first.

To distinguish **movement from compression**, follow neighboring air elements over a cycle. If they travel together, the region moves while the gaps between them change little. If they move differently, those gaps close and open strongly. A point can have little movement of its own while its neighbors produce a large change in compression around it.

The same physical region can therefore matter differently to the two modes. Added effective mass has more influence where a mode moves strongly. Added springiness has more influence where the mode compresses and expands the air strongly. The one-third /a/ marker, two-thirds /i/ marker, and lip-end /u/ marker locate three regions to compare. Their positions are measured from the glottis, so each refers to the same place in both patterns.

sections.title: /u/ loads the moving lip end
teaching: The /u/ constriction acts at the lip end of the model. This is the free end, where both the F1-like and F2-like modes have substantial movement. **Free-end loading** means increasing the effective mass involved in that movement. The larger drawn masses represent greater inertia, rather than individual air molecules becoming heavier.

Greater effective mass makes the motion respond more slowly when the restoring properties are otherwise comparable. At the lips, movement is important for both modes, so the mass effect dominates both. **F1 falls and F2 falls** relative to the uniform reference. The shared direction follows from the same local mass change acting where both modes move strongly.

sections.title: /i/ has opposite effects on F1 and F2
teaching: The /i/ constriction is near two-thirds of the distance from the glottis toward the lips. It affects the same region of air in both mode patterns. A constriction can increase both local effective mass and springiness, but the two effects matter differently according to how each mode moves or compresses that region.

For the first mode, the **mass effect** is stronger. The air takes part in substantial movement, so greater inertia makes the cycle slower and F1 falls. For the second mode, the **springiness effect** is stronger. Compression and expansion are important there, so a stronger restoring effect makes the cycle faster and F2 rises.

The result is lower F1 and higher F2 relative to the uniform reference. Increasing mass and stiffness in one region does not mean that their effects cancel. Each mode is affected according to its own movement and compression at that location.

sections.title: /a/ reverses the two effects
teaching: The /a/ constriction lies near one-third of the distance from the glottis toward the lips. Moving the constriction changes which region of each mode is affected. The rules for mass and stiffness stay the same, but the local movement and compression differ from those at the /i/ location.

For the first mode, **springiness** is the stronger effect at this location. The mode strongly involves compression there, so increased restoring stiffness makes the cycle faster and F1 rises. For the second mode, the **mass effect** is stronger. Greater inertia slows the movement and F2 falls.

The result is higher F1 and lower F2 relative to the uniform reference. This reverses the /i/ pattern because the constriction affects a different part of each coordinated movement. The cause runs from location, to movement or compression in that mode, to the effect of mass or stiffness on its frequency.

sections.title: Mass, stiffness, position, and frequency
teaching: Greater **mass** slows a system’s response to the same restoring force, so frequency falls when stiffness stays unchanged. Greater **stiffness** supplies a stronger restoring force for the same displacement, so frequency rises when mass stays unchanged. These are different causes, and identifying what changed establishes the basic direction of the effect.

Within a larger system, the importance of a change also depends on location. Added mass matters most where the mode moves strongly. Added stiffness matters most where the material stretches or compresses strongly. Neighbors moving together can travel far with little change in their separation. Neighbors moving differently can strongly change their separation near a point with little movement. Each mode therefore has its own pattern of sensitivity along the system.

The three vowel comparisons follow that local reasoning. At the lip-end /u/ region, the first two modes both have a strong mass effect, so F1 and F2 fall. Near two-thirds of the distance from the glottis, the /i/ change slows the first mode through mass and speeds the second through springiness. Near one-third, the /a/ change speeds the first through springiness and slows the second through mass. The constriction affects different parts of the mode patterns while the underlying frequency rules remain the same.

An allowed mode must also fit the conditions at the ends. A chain of separate masses has one mode per movable mass in the modeled direction, generally without exact whole-number frequency spacing. An ideal continuous fixed–fixed string fits half-waves and has whole-number harmonics. An ideal fixed–free system fits odd numbers of quarter-waves and has odd-multiple resonances. The endpoints determine which patterns fit, and changes in mass or stiffness influence how fast those patterns repeat.

sections.title: Compression and motion alternate in an air column
teaching: The moving air in the uniform tube labeled Schwa is the reference. The other rows separately show Mode 1 at F1, Mode 2 at F2, and Mode 3 at F3. The blue circles represent air elements moving along a tube closed at the left and open at the right. These are different movement patterns of the same air system.

When neighboring elements bunch together, the air is **compressed**. When they spread apart, the air is rarefied, meaning less densely packed. The change in compression produces a restoring effect, while the moving air’s inertia keeps it moving. Their interaction supports the repeated movement back and forth along the tube.

Large movement and large changes in compression occur in different regions of a standing mode. Neighbors can travel together while their gaps change little. Elsewhere, different neighboring movements make the gaps close and open strongly, even near a point whose own movement is small. Following the change over a cycle distinguishes the distance an air element travels from the changing distance between elements.

The closed end limits air displacement, while the open end permits strong movement. Higher modes have more alternating regions along the same tube. F1, F2, and F3 identify different resonances, rather than separate air streams. A vowel can therefore contain several frequency components at the same time.

sections.title: Masses and Springs in Speech Production
Mass, stiffness, position, and frequency
teaching: **Mass** is the part of the system that has to be moved. A moving mass tends to keep moving, and changing its motion requires a force. Increasing the mass makes it harder to speed up, slow down, and reverse. If the spring’s stiffness stays the same, each back-and-forth cycle takes longer, so **frequency falls**. Frequency means how many complete cycles occur in a given time.

**Stiffness** describes how strongly the spring pushes or pulls back when it is squeezed or stretched. A stiffer spring provides a stronger return toward the resting position. If the mass stays the same, the system returns and reverses more quickly, so **frequency rises**. The two changes have different effects because one changes how hard the moving part is to move, while the other changes how strongly it is brought back.

A system with several masses can move in several organized patterns called **normal modes**. Within one mode, the masses repeat their movements at the same frequency, but different parts can move in opposite directions. In the chains considered here, each added mass adds one more independent pattern. A higher mode has more changes between regions that move one way and regions that move the other way.

Where a change is made matters. Adding mass has a strong effect where that mode moves a lot, because the system has to move the extra load there. Increasing stiffness has a strong effect where the spring stretches or compresses a lot. In these ideal standing-wave patterns, the places with greatest movement alternate with places of greatest stretching or compression. The same location can therefore matter differently to different modes.

The restrictions at the ends are called **boundary conditions**. A string fixed at both ends fits whole numbers of half-waves, giving consecutive harmonics. An ideal air column fixed at one end and free at the other fits odd numbers of quarter-waves, giving odd-multiple resonances. These simple relations apply to the ideal examples. A chain with a finite number of masses generally does not have exact whole-number frequency ratios, and a vocal tract with changes in shape does not keep the simple uniform-tube pattern.

sections.title: One more mass, one more mode
teaching: A **normal mode** is an organized way for the whole chain to move. One mass between fixed ends has one such pattern. A two-mass chain has two, a three-mass chain has three, and the relationship continues through the six-mass chain. The added pattern belongs to the whole system. It is not a new motion assigned only to the mass that was added.

In **Mode 1**, the moving masses are on the same side of their resting positions together. They pass through rest, move to the other side, and reverse together. They can move different distances while still following the same timing. Higher modes divide the chain into groups that move in opposite directions. Moving across a row introduces more of these changes in direction and a higher frequency.

The fixed endpoints stay in place as the masses move between them. Some modes also have a mass that stays still inside the chain while its neighbors move. That mass’s location is part of the pattern, so seeing one still mass does not mean the whole system has stopped. The empty part of the chart corresponds to modes that the smaller chains do not have.

The masses and the strength of the connections are kept equal in these comparisons. The largest movements are also enlarged to the same displayed size, and colors identify the mode number. Comparing frequencies requires following how quickly the motion repeats, rather than deciding which picture looks tallest. These finite chains generally have frequencies that are not exact multiples of the lowest frequency. Their mode counts and an ideal string’s harmonic frequency pattern are different facts.

sections.title: Why fixed–fixed frequencies are integer multiples
teaching: A string fixed at both ends cannot move sideways at either endpoint. A place that remains still in a vibration pattern is called a **node**. The simplest mode bows out between the endpoints, with its greatest movement between the two nodes. This makes one **half-wave**, a section of the pattern from one node to the next.

**Mode 2** fits two half-waves into the same string. The middle stays still while the two sides move in opposite directions. As the string passes through its resting line, the two sides continue to the opposite sides and reverse. The next modes contain three, four, and five half-waves, each with more moving regions separated by internal nodes.

Fitting more sections into the same length makes each wavelength shorter. With the speed of the wave unchanged, shorter wavelengths correspond to faster vibrations. The frequencies are therefore whole-number multiples of the **fundamental**, which is the lowest allowed frequency. Both even and odd multiples fit because every whole half-wave ends at another node.

The numbered sections count the parts of each standing-wave shape. All five modes contain a first half-wave. Only modes with enough sections contain a second, third, fourth, or fifth. The sections stay at fixed positions along the string as the material moves up and down. Counting them explains the allowed shapes and frequencies, not how many cycles have already happened.

sections.title: A fixed–fixed string combines harmonics
teaching: A string can move in several modes at once. At each point, the movements contributed by the different modes **add together** to give the string’s actual position. When contributions point the same way, their effects become larger together. When they point in opposite directions, they partly cancel. The combined shape changes because the component modes do not all complete their cycles at the same rate.

All five modes keep both endpoints fixed. Each moving region passes through its resting position, reaches the other side, and reverses. The higher harmonics complete more cycles during the same interval. Slowing every mode by the same factor makes that relationship visible without changing which mode is faster.

The **spectrum** describes the motion measured at the marked point on the combined string. Its horizontal direction gives frequency, meaning how fast a component repeats. Its vertical direction gives amplitude, meaning how strongly the component appears in that measurement. A line farther to the right has a higher frequency. A taller line has a larger amplitude. Those are separate properties.

The five peaks are consecutive harmonics of the illustrated **100 Hz fundamental**. They have equal heights because the component strengths were adjusted to make their contributions equal at the selected measurement point. Equal heights are a choice in this demonstration. Another measurement location can represent the components differently because the modes move different amounts at different places. The complex shape belongs to one moving string, while the spectrum identifies the frequencies contributing to that motion.

sections.title: A membrane combines spatial modes
teaching: A **membrane** is a surface, so its movement can be divided across two directions. All outside edges remain fixed while the interior rises above and falls below its resting surface. The simplest mode has one broad moving region. Other modes divide the membrane into two regions in one direction, two in the other direction, four regions across both directions, or three regions along one direction.

Neighboring regions in these divided patterns move on opposite sides of rest. A region that is raised moves downward, passes through the resting surface, and becomes lowered. The neighboring region makes the opposite change. The lines separating those regions stay still within that mode. The shape is therefore organized by fixed places even while the membrane continues moving.

The combined surface is made by **adding the movements of all five modes at each point**. Some movements strengthen one another, while others cancel partly. This produces changing bumps and dips that can look different from any one component mode. The combined panel uses a smaller vertical display scale so the result fits, so its apparent height cannot be compared directly with the enlarged individual panels.

The spectrum measures movement at one marked point. Frequency is shown horizontally and relative amplitude vertically. The five peak heights were made equal at that point. Their evenly spaced frequencies were also **assigned for the illustration**. They are not the natural resonance frequencies of the rectangular membrane. The example shows how different patterns can combine into one motion and be identified in a spectrum, while the membrane’s natural frequency pattern remains a separate issue.

sections.title: One fixed end and one free end
teaching: A **fixed–free string** has different restrictions at its two ends. The fixed bottom stays still and is a node. The free top moves through the largest back-and-forth distance and is an **antinode**, a place of greatest movement in the pattern. The simplest allowed shape goes from a node to an antinode. That section is a **quarter-wave**.

The next allowed pattern must still start at a node and end at an antinode. Adding two more quarter-waves keeps those endpoint requirements while adding more movement and stationary places inside the string. The allowed patterns therefore contain odd numbers of quarter-waves and produce **odd harmonics**. The second available mode is the third harmonic. Mode number counts the patterns that are allowed, while harmonic number compares frequency with the fundamental.

The individual curves cross their resting positions and reverse while the fixed bottom remains still. The lower spectrum shows frequency horizontally and amplitude vertically for a mixture measured at the free end. Its equal peak heights come from equal excitation in this setup. The slow playback preserves the relative speeds of the component modes.

The fixed–fixed and fixed–free examples have been **tuned separately** to the same displayed fundamental. If a string kept the same length and wave speed while one fixed end became free, the fundamental would become half as high. Giving both demonstrations the same fundamental therefore also involves a change in length or wave speed. Matching frequency labels cannot establish that changing an endpoint has no effect.

sections.title: Why fixed–free frequencies are odd multiples
teaching: A **quarter-wave** is the section between a node and an antinode. The fixed bottom of each illustrated string has to be a node, and the free top has to be an antinode. One quarter-wave fits those restrictions. Adding a pair of quarter-waves adds an internal change from antinode to node and back to antinode while preserving the required top.

The four modes contain **one, three, five, and seven quarter-waves** in the same length. More sections mean a shorter wavelength and a faster vibration when wave speed is unchanged. The second mode is the third harmonic, the third mode is the fifth harmonic, and the fourth mode is the seventh harmonic. An even number of quarter-waves would finish at a node, which does not match the free top.

The numbered sections show how these counts build up. Every mode contains the first section. Only the higher modes have the additional sections, and only the fourth mode contains the sixth and seventh. These numbers describe places within a standing-wave shape. The moving parts reverse as time passes, while the divisions of the pattern stay at the same positions along the string.

sections.title: Count quarter-waves from the boundary conditions
teaching: To read the four **fixed–free patterns**, begin with the endpoint requirements. The bottom is a node because it cannot move, and the top is an antinode because it is free to move. Following the shape from a node to an antinode, or from an antinode to a node, covers a quarter-wave. The four shapes contain one, three, five, and seven of these sections.

The shape with more sections fits a shorter wavelength into the same total length and oscillates faster when wave speed stays the same. **Mode number** tells where an allowed pattern comes in the sequence. **Harmonic number** tells how its frequency relates to the fundamental. The fourth allowed pattern is the seventh harmonic because the fixed–free restrictions allow odd quarter-wave counts. The labels can be understood from the shape without treating fourth mode as fourth harmonic.

sections.title: Air in a fixed–free tube has modes
teaching: Air can move and resist compression, so it can be represented with **masses and springs**. The masses stand for air that has to be moved. The springs stand for the force that pushes compressed or spread-out air back toward its usual condition. In the simplified tract, the glottal end at the left is constrained and the lip end at the right is open and free.

The air elements move **along the tube**, back and forth around their usual positions. This is called longitudinal motion. When neighboring elements come closer together, the region is compressed. When they spread farther apart, the region becomes less dense, or rarefied. The repeating movement is an acoustic vibration. It does not mean that each element travels steadily from one end of the tract to the other.

The lowest organized pattern is labeled **F1-like**, and the next is **F2-like**. F1 and F2 are resonances of the air in the tract, frequencies at which its corresponding patterns can respond strongly. In the uniform reference tube, which has the same shape along its length, the second mode vibrates three times as fast as the first. Changing the shape along the tract changes that simple reference pattern.

The /a/ marker lies about one third of the way from the glottis, the /i/ marker about two thirds along, and the /u/ marker at the lips. These are the same physical places in both rows. To understand a narrowing there, compare how much the air moves and compresses at that place in each mode.

sections.title: Compression and motion alternate in an air column
teaching: **Air movement** and **compression** are related but different. Following one air element shows how far it travels back and forth from its usual position. Comparing neighboring elements shows whether the gaps between them become smaller or larger. Small gaps mean compression, while larger gaps mean rarefaction. A place can have little movement of its own while the air around it bunches together and spreads apart.

The **Schwa** row shows the moving reference for the uniform tube. The three lower rows separate the patterns labeled F1, F2, and F3. In each pattern, elements move along the tube, pass back through their usual positions, and reverse. The top row also moves, so it is not a motionless reference image.

The closed end at the left limits movement, and the open end at the right allows strong movement. Inside the tube, the places that move most alternate with places where compression changes most. The higher modes add more of these alternating regions within the same length. Separating the rows makes it possible to compare what happens at one location for different resonances of the same air column.

sections.title: Vowel shape locates a constriction
teaching: **Vowels** differ in how the tongue and lips shape the air passage. High and low describe tongue height, while front and back describe where the tongue is positioned along the mouth. A change in position changes where the tract becomes narrow. The location of that narrowing affects how the air can vibrate.

The vowels in **dean** and **dune** are both high, but they have different shapes. Dean is high and front. Its marked constriction lies about two thirds of the way from the glottis to the lips. Dune is high and back, with its marked constriction at the lips. Calling both high therefore does not make their tract shapes the same.

**Dan** is the low front example and **Don** is the low back example. Don’s constriction is marked about one third of the way from the glottis. **Done** is central and is labeled No constriction, providing the relatively open comparison. Dan is shown as low and front without a numbered constriction position.

The fractions describe distance along the air path starting at the glottis. A narrowing at one third of the length affects a different part of a mode from a narrowing at two thirds or at the lips. Tongue-position labels describe the articulation. To explain the acoustic effect, relate the narrowing to how much each mode moves or compresses the air there.

sections.title: Why a constriction can raise one formant and lower another
teaching: A **constriction** is a narrowing of the air passage. Moving the tongue changes where that narrowing lies, as the two tract shapes illustrate. In the lecture’s account, bunching air increases its local density and its mass-like effect on movement. Compression also increases the air’s resistance to further compression, giving it a stronger spring-like effect.

The mass-like effect matters where the air moves a lot. A greater moving load is harder to accelerate and reverse, so that effect tends to slow the vibration. The spring-like effect matters where the air compresses and spreads apart a lot. A stronger push back toward the usual spacing tends to speed up the vibration.

Increasing both effects does not make them cancel automatically. The places with greatest movement are not the same as the places with greatest compression change in these modes. A group of air elements can move together over a large distance without greatly changing the gaps between them. Elsewhere, neighboring elements can approach and separate around a place that moves very little.

The balance has to be considered for **each mode separately**. At one tract location, movement can be more important for F1 while compression is more important for F2. The same narrowing can then slow one resonance and speed the other. That difference follows from where the air moves and compresses in the two patterns, while the basic effects of mass and stiffness stay the same.

sections.title: Compression and motion alternate in an air column
teaching: To see where **movement matters most**, follow how far an air element travels back and forth over a cycle. Adding load in a place with a large movement strongly affects the air that the mode has to move. To see where **compression matters most**, follow the gaps between neighbors. Large changes in spacing reveal a strong spring-like part of the oscillation even if an element near that region moves only a little.

The F1, F2, and F3 rows place their strongest movement and compression changes at different positions. The higher modes divide the tube into more alternating regions. A location with large movement in the first mode can have a different role in the second or third. The location alone is therefore not enough to predict a change without also identifying the mode.

The moving Schwa row supplies the uniform-tube reference, and the lower rows separate its resonance patterns. The left end restricts movement, while the open right end permits it. Following several moments shows the elements reversing around their usual places and the air becoming compressed or spread out. Both observations are needed to explain what a local change would do.

sections.title: Air in a fixed–free tube has modes
teaching: **F1 and F2** refer to different resonance patterns of the same air column. The glottal end is constrained at the left, and the lip end is free at the right. Both illustrated modes allow substantial movement near the lips. The second mode also has more internal changes between regions that move and regions that compress.

The /a/, /i/, and /u/ markers identify the same locations in both rows. The back marker is about one third of the way from the glottis, the front marker about two thirds, and the lip marker is at the free end. Comparing one marker across the rows shows why a narrowing there can affect F1 and F2 differently.

Follow the air elements to see the amount of movement, and compare the gaps between them to see compression and rarefaction. If a change mainly loads moving air, it tends to slow that mode. If it mainly strengthens the return from compression, it tends to speed that mode. The reference second mode cycles three times as fast as the first in this ideal uniform tube. The direction of a change is explained by how the altered region takes part in each pattern.

sections.title: /u/ loads the moving lip end
teaching: The /u/ model places extra **mass-like loading near the lips**, the free end of the air column. The larger masses show where the load is added. Both the F1-like and F2-like modes move strongly near this end, so both have to move that added load back and forth.

Extra moving mass makes the air harder to accelerate and reverse. When this effect is more important than the stiffness change, completing a cycle takes longer. The reasoning therefore gives **F1 down and F2 down**. The directions match because movement is important near the lip end in both modes.

The explanation connects the position of the change to the movement of each mode, then connects the added load to slower vibration. It does not use a rule that every narrowing lowers every frequency. The source supplies a simplified illustration and the predicted directions. It does not supply numerical before-and-after measurements from a completed experiment.

sections.title: /i/ has opposite effects on F1 and F2
teaching: The /i/ model places the narrowing near the **front of the tract**, about two thirds of the way from the glottis to the lips. The marked region is in the same place in both rows. That place has different roles in the two patterns, so the same narrowing can lead to different frequency changes.

For the F1-like mode, movement is the more important part of the comparison. Loading that moving air makes it harder to accelerate and reverse. The vibration slows, so **F1 falls**. For the F2-like mode, the region’s compression changes are more important. Increasing the spring-like push back makes the vibration faster, so **F2 rises**.

The result is the **low-F1, high-F2** pattern. Both mass-like and spring-like effects can increase, but they do not matter equally in each mode. The answer depends on the movement and compression at the changed location, rather than assuming that one narrowing must move every resonance in the same direction.

The movement and the highlighted region illustrate this physical reasoning, and the source gives the two predicted directions. They are not numerical measurements of how far the formants moved. The claim supported here is why the directions differ in this simplified comparison.

sections.title: /a/ reverses the two effects
teaching: The /a/ comparison places the narrowing farther back, about **one third of the way from the glottis**. Moving the narrowing changes which part of each mode is affected. The basic rule remains that extra moving mass slows a vibration, while a stronger restoring push speeds it.

For the F1-like mode, the changed back region is important to compression. The increased spring-like effect is the more important change, so the air returns and reverses more quickly and **F1 rises**. For the F2-like mode, movement is more important there. Loading that moving air makes its cycle slower, so **F2 falls**.

This gives the reverse of the /i/ pattern. The two cases can be explained with the same physical rules because the narrowing is in a different place. First locate the changed region, then compare movement and compression in each mode. A description such as high or low vowel does not by itself explain both frequency arrows.

The marked sections show the location of the change, while the moving masses illustrate the two modes. The source gives a **qualitative prediction**, meaning the direction of the change. It does not give a measured numerical size for the formant shifts.

sections.title: Compression and motion alternate in an air column
teaching: **F1, F2, and F3 are resonances of one air column**. Each label refers to a different organized pattern of vibration available to the same air. The separate rows make those patterns easier to compare. They do not represent separate streams traveling through the mouth.

The air elements move along the tube and reverse around their usual positions. Their changing spacing makes regions more compressed or more spread out. The Schwa row also moves and provides the uniform-tube reference. The closed left end restricts movement, the open right end permits it, and higher modes have more alternating regions inside the same tract.

A change at one position can affect several resonances differently because each mode moves and compresses the air differently there. The labels F1, F2, and F3 identify which patterns and frequencies are being described. To explain the effect of the change, follow the air’s movement and compression for each of those patterns.

sections.title: The source supplies harmonics and the filter shapes their heights
teaching: **Source–filter theory** explains a voiced vowel by separating what the vocal folds supply from what the air passage does to that sound. Repeated vibration at the glottis provides the **source**. The vocal tract acts as the **filter** because its shape makes the air respond more strongly at some frequencies than at others. Those strongly responding frequency regions are its resonances, called **formants**.

The repeating source contains **harmonics**, components at whole-number multiples of its fundamental frequency. The fundamental is labeled **F0** and describes how fast the source repeats. In the illustrated source spectrum, the lines are evenly spaced. Their horizontal positions show frequency, and their heights show amplitude, or strength. The equal heights simplify the example so the filter’s effect is easy to see.

Passing through the vocal tract changes which of those components are strong or weak. A harmonic near a formant becomes more prominent than one in a region where the tract responds less strongly. The frequencies supplied by the source keep their spacing. What changes in this comparison is the **pattern of line heights**, not the source’s repetition rate.

The broad shape traced by those heights is called the **spectral envelope**. It shows which frequency regions the tract favors. The schwa example has groups around four labeled formants, F1 through F4, with the strongest group in the low-frequency region. Many harmonic frequencies are still present, so the vowel is not made from a single frequency or just four isolated tones.

**F0 and F1 describe different things**. F0 comes from the repeating source. F1 is the lowest tract resonance, with F2, F3, and F4 identifying higher resonances. Their values in the drawing belong to a simplified schwa comparison, not one fixed set for every speaker. Keeping the source and the filter separate explains how vowels can differ in their pattern of strong frequencies even when their source spacing stays the same.

sections.title: The /i/ filter keeps F1 low and F2 high
teaching: The /i/ pattern has a **low F1 and a high F2**. Its first strong group of harmonics is near the low-frequency end of the spectrum, while its next strong group is much farther to the right. The region between them is weak. Further groups occur around the higher formants, F3 and F4.

The source keeps the same regularly spaced harmonics as the other vowel comparisons. The tract changes how strong those harmonics become. This makes the effect of the **vocal tract filter** visible on its own. The front constriction account explains why the first resonance is low and the second is high by comparing where movement or compression matters in each mode.

The horizontal position of a line gives its **frequency**, and the height of the line gives its **amplitude**. A tall line near the left is strong but still low in frequency. A shorter line farther to the right has a higher frequency even though it is weaker. Greater height therefore does not mean a higher pitch or wider spacing between source harmonics.

The formants describe the broad pattern of strong and weak frequency regions. The individual narrow lines are the harmonics that show that pattern. The illustrated formant values describe this particular /i/ filter. The important distinction is the low first resonance and high second resonance, not a claim that every speaker must have the same numbers or that the vowel contains only two frequencies.

sections.title: The /a/ filter raises F1 and lowers F2
teaching: The /a/ pattern has a **higher F1 and a lower F2** than the /i/ comparison. The first strong frequency region is higher, and the second is lower, so the first two resonant regions are closer together. Groups around F3 and F4 remain at higher frequencies.

The tract changes the **broad pattern of harmonic strengths** while the source remains regularly spaced. On the spectrum, moving a formant concerns where a favored frequency region lies along the horizontal direction. Changing the amplitude of a harmonic concerns how tall that line is. The same source can therefore show a different vowel pattern when the tract shape changes.

A formant can lie **between two harmonics**. The tract can respond most strongly at a frequency that the source does not supply as an exact harmonic. The neighboring supplied harmonics still become strong because they are near that region. Their heights reveal parts of the filter’s response, while the exact point between them has no source line to show it directly.

This is why a formant and a harmonic are different labels. A formant describes a resonance of the tract. A harmonic describes a component supplied by the repeating source. Changing the resonance does not require moving the source’s harmonic positions. The drawing uses a simplified set of /a/ formants to show these relationships, rather than specifying the same frequencies for every production of the vowel.

sections.title: A spectrogram places successive spectra in time
teaching: A **spectrum** shows how strong the different frequency components are for one short moment. A **spectrogram** follows that information across time. The small spectra show successive examples of /i/ followed by examples of /a/. Their different shapes show a changing pattern of strong and weak frequency regions.

In a spectrum, **frequency runs horizontally** and amplitude runs vertically. To place that information in a spectrogram, frequency is placed **vertically**, with low frequencies near the bottom and high frequencies near the top. A low-frequency peak becomes a mark low in the corresponding vertical strip. A high-frequency peak becomes a mark higher in that strip.

The spectrogram’s horizontal direction now represents **time**. Placing the strips in order shows how the sound changes from left to right. Moving right across a spectrum means moving to a higher frequency, but moving right across a spectrogram means moving to a later moment. Reading the axes tells which kind of change is being shown.

**Darkness gives amplitude** in this grayscale spectrogram. High amplitude becomes black, medium amplitude becomes gray, and low amplitude becomes white. A tall peak in a spectrum therefore produces a dark mark at that frequency in its time strip. The mark’s vertical position gives frequency, while its darkness gives strength. A darker mark is not automatically a higher-frequency mark.

As /i/ changes toward /a/, the **F1 band rises and the F2 band falls**. They begin farther apart and become closer together. Higher formant bands remain above them with smaller changes. Their positions show the changing resonances of the tract, while their darkness carries the amplitude information that was represented by heights in the individual spectra.

sections.title: Reflection prompt
Wide harmonic spacing makes formants harder to identify
teaching: The source harmonics show the vocal tract’s response at the frequencies that the source supplies. If the harmonics are close together, many of them fall around each formant. Their heights can show the rise toward a strong region and the fall away from it. This makes the broad formant pattern easier to recognize.

Increasing **F0** spreads the harmonics farther apart. Fewer source frequencies now fall around each resonance. A formant can lie in a gap between them, so the sound gives less information about the exact shape of that strong region. This is called **sparser sampling** here: the same filter is represented by fewer supplied frequencies.

The comparison keeps the **vocal tract filter the same** and changes the source pitch. The three spectra show increasingly separated harmonic lines under the same formant pattern. The spectrograms show the corresponding difficulty. With closely spaced harmonics, the formant regions are easier to follow as bands. With wider spacing, isolated harmonic traces can stand out more clearly than the broad formant regions.

A strong harmonic is not necessarily sitting exactly at a formant. It may be strong because it is near the formant, while the resonance itself lies between source frequencies. Seeing a single prominent line therefore gives less information than seeing several nearby lines trace the shape of a resonance.

The toddler and soprano examples apply this issue to **high-pitched voices**. A higher source pitch means wider harmonic spacing, which can make the tract’s formants harder to identify. It does not by itself show that F1 or F2 has moved upward. The source pitch determines which frequencies are available to show the filter’s response, while the tract’s shape determines the resonances being revealed.

sections.title: Homework 4 lab reminder
Speech → Neural Networks
Five membrane modes combine into one motion
teaching: A **mode** is a pattern in which the whole membrane moves. The outside edges are fixed, but the material between them can rise, return through its resting position, and move downward. Different modes divide that movement into different regions. Where two neighboring regions move in opposite directions, a stationary line lies between them. That line is a **node**.

The two numbers in a mode label describe divisions along the two directions of the surface. In (1, 1), one broad region moves together. In (2, 1), the surface divides into two oppositely moving regions along one direction; in (1, 2), the division runs along the other direction. The (2, 2) pattern divides it both ways, producing four regions. The (3, 1) pattern has three regions along one direction. These are different movements of the same connected membrane, rather than separate pieces of material.

When the modes occur together, their movements add at each point. Two contributions pointing upward reinforce each other. An upward and a downward contribution partly cancel. Because the modes repeat at different rates, their relative positions keep changing, and the combined surface keeps changing shape. The separate patterns are still parts of that combined movement. This addition is called **superposition**.

The **spectrum** separates the movement recorded at the marked pickup into its frequency components. Frequency runs horizontally, while peak height shows the strength of a component at that position. The five peaks are equally high because the component movements were adjusted to give equal readings there. Another position can move by a different amount in each mode. Equal peaks at one pickup therefore do not mean equal movement everywhere.

The illustration assigns the frequencies 100, 200, 300, 400, and 500 Hz to make an evenly spaced harmonic example. Those frequencies were chosen for teaching; they are not the membrane’s calculated natural frequencies. Playback is slowed so the movement is visible, and the combined panel is drawn on a smaller vertical scale so it fits. The labels describe the intended repetition rates, while the screen settings help make those movements readable.

sections.title: A fixed end and a free end select odd harmonics
teaching: A **fixed end** must stay in place, so it is a displacement node. A **free end** can move, so the allowed patterns put a displacement antinode there.
