An antinode is a position with a large back-and-forth movement over the cycle. It still passes through its resting position; it does not remain at its farthest point throughout the motion.

The lowest mode grows from no movement at the fixed bottom to strong movement at the free top. Higher modes fit more changes of direction into the same length. Different regions then move on opposite sides of their resting positions, with nodes between them. When the motion reverses, the moving regions switch sides while the nodes remain in place.

The frequencies shown are 100, 300, 500, and 700 Hz. These are the **odd harmonics** of the lowest frequency. The second allowed mode is three times as fast as the first, so it is called the third harmonic. Mode number counts the allowed patterns in order. Harmonic number compares the frequency with the fundamental. These numbers differ because the even-harmonic patterns would not give the required fixed end and free end.

The spectrum records the four modes together at the free end. All four have strong movement there, and their amounts were chosen to produce equal peaks at that pickup. The video slows the motion for viewing without changing which mode is faster than another.

The fixed–fixed and fixed–free demonstrations were separately adjusted to give the same labelled fundamental. That is different from changing just the boundary. If length and wave speed stay fixed, replacing a fixed end with a free end lowers the fundamental to half its former frequency. A comparison must keep those conditions the same to show what changing the endpoint alone does.

sections.title: Quarter-wavelength packets explain the allowed modes
teaching: A **quarter-wavelength** connects a node to an antinode. One quarter-wave therefore fits the simplest pattern between a stationary fixed end and a freely moving end. It gives the first mode without an extra stationary point inside the string.

Adding another quarter-wave would finish at a node. That would be appropriate for a second fixed end, but it would not give the free-end movement required here. Adding two quarter-waves brings the pattern back to an antinode. Each additional pair adds another change of direction inside the string while leaving the correct kind of movement at its ends.

The allowed patterns therefore contain one, three, five, and seven quarter-waves. More pieces have to fit inside the same length, so each wavelength becomes shorter. With wave speed unchanged, shorter waves repeat faster. The odd frequency pattern follows from the **endpoint conditions**, rather than from an arbitrary decision to leave out some frequencies.

The numbered pieces divide the shape of the standing wave. They do not move one after another up the string. The material moves back and forth, and its stationary points remain in the same places. The higher modes are more detailed patterns of that movement within the same space.

sections.title: Air moves longitudinally in vocal-tract modes
teaching: Air can be understood through two familiar properties. It has **mass**, so moving air tends to keep moving and resists changes in its motion. It can also be compressed, so air pushed into a smaller space pushes back. The mass-and-spring chain represents these two parts of the acoustic system. Its masses stand for the air’s tendency to keep moving, and its springs stand for the return toward the usual spacing.

The circles move along the tube, rather than sideways like a string. This is **longitudinal motion**. When neighbors move closer, the air is compressed. When their spacing increases, it is rarefied. Each part moves back and forth around its usual position. Sound therefore does not require the same air particles to travel continuously from the glottis out of the mouth.

The glottal end is constrained and the lip end is open in this simple model. **Mode 1**, labelled F1-like, has the broadest pattern and the lowest resonance. **Mode 2**, labelled F2-like, fits an extra alternation into the same air column. In the ideal uniform-tube comparison, Mode 2 repeats three times as fast as Mode 1. This relation describes the reference example, rather than every possible finite chain or vowel shape.

The /a/ marker lies one third of the way from the glottis, /i/ lies two thirds along, and /u/ lies at the lips. Each location takes part in both modes. A location can move strongly in one mode but undergo stronger compression changes in another. Comparing those two roles explains how a narrowing there can affect **F1 and F2**, the first two tract resonances, differently.

sections.title: Track air motion separately from compression
teaching: **Air movement** and **air compression** are different things to track. An element can travel a long way while its neighbors travel with it, leaving their gaps nearly unchanged. Elsewhere, neighbors can move toward and away from one another, changing the gaps substantially. The first case emphasizes how far the air moves. The second emphasizes how much it is squeezed and spread out.

To follow movement, watch one circle as it moves to one side, returns through its usual position, and reverses. To follow compression, watch the spacing of several neighboring circles. A crowded region is compressed at that instant. When the gaps widen later in the cycle, it becomes less compressed or more spread out. This changing spacing supplies the spring-like restoring action.

The closed end restricts movement, while the open end allows a larger movement. In the lowest mode, strong compression lies toward the constrained end. Higher modes fit more alternations into the same tube, so the locations of strong movement and strong compression change. A location that is important for one kind of change in Mode 1 can be important for another kind in Mode 2.

The moving schwa reference and the **F1, F2, and F3** rows describe the same air system through different resonance patterns. The rows separate those patterns so their local behavior can be compared. A constriction can matter strongly to the moving mass in one mode and to the compressed air in another. That is why its formant effects depend on the mode as well as the location.

sections.title: Compare positions within an air mode
teaching: A marked position in the air column must be followed through its movement, rather than judged from one still moment. Watching one element shows its back-and-forth movement. Watching neighboring elements shows whether their spacing changes. A region can have strong motion with little change in spacing, or strong compression changes with little motion at its center.

Where air moves strongly, increasing its effective mass makes that movement harder to change and reverse. The cycle then takes longer, so the resonance tends to fall. Where air compresses strongly, increasing its **stiffness** makes it push back more strongly toward its usual spacing. The cycle becomes faster when that effect is more important, so the resonance tends to rise.

The same position can behave differently in **Mode 1, Mode 2, and Mode 3**. Each mode places its regions of movement and compression differently along the tube. Explaining a change therefore means identifying the location, identifying the mode, and connecting its local movement to the mass or spring effect that matters most there.

sections.title: Vowel positions change where the tract is narrowed
teaching: Vowels differ in the shape of the air passage above the glottis. **High and low** describe tongue height. **Front and back** describe where the tongue is positioned along the mouth. Moving the tongue and lips changes where the passage becomes narrow, which changes how its air can resonate.

The vowel in dean is high and front. Its marked narrowing is about two thirds of the way from the glottis toward the lips. The vowel in dune is high and back, and the highlighted narrowing is at the lips. These vowels share the description high, but they narrow different parts of the air passage. The shared description does not make their resonance patterns the same.

The vowel in done is central and serves as the relatively unconstricted reference. Dan is the low-front comparison, while Don is the low-back comparison. The narrowing marked for Don is about one third of the way from the glottis. This lies farther back along the tract than the front narrowing marked for dean.

The fractions start at the glottis and follow the passage toward the lips. Their purpose is to locate the changed region of air. That location matters because each mode has its own pattern of movement and compression. The tongue description identifies the shape change; the air-mode pattern explains why that change alters a particular formant.

sections.title: A constriction changes inertia and restoring stiffness
teaching: A **constriction** is a narrowing of the air passage. In the lecture’s mass-and-spring explanation, it changes both the mass-like behavior of the moving air and the stiffness of air that is being compressed. These changes have different effects on vibration, so predicting the result requires knowing which one matters more at that location.

**Mass** tends to keep moving. When a region moves strongly in a mode, increasing its effective mass makes that movement harder to speed up and turn around. A cycle takes longer when this effect is strongest, so frequency falls. The explanation runs from the location of strong motion to more resistance to changing that motion, and then to a slower vibration.

**Stiffness** describes how strongly the compressed air pushes back. Where the spacing between neighbors changes greatly, a stronger spring-like response returns them toward their usual spacing more quickly. A cycle becomes faster when this effect is strongest, so frequency rises.

The two changes do not simply cancel. Air does not move and compress equally at every point, and those patterns differ between modes. The same narrowing can therefore act mainly like added mass for one resonance and mainly like a stronger spring for another. Its location within each pattern explains the direction of the formant change.

sections.title: Use both modes to interpret the same tract location
teaching: **Mode 1 and Mode 2** are two movements of the same air column. Both have a constrained glottal end and an open lip end. The second mode fits an additional alternation inside that length, so its regions of movement and compression are arranged differently from those of the first.

A narrowing occupies the same physical location for both modes. What differs is how each mode uses that location. Near the lips, both move the air strongly. Farther inside the tube, the same region can have strong motion in one mode and stronger compression changes in the other. A single change in the tract can therefore produce different changes in F1 and F2.

The back, front, and lip markers make the location specific. Strong movement makes the mass-like effect important; stronger resistance to turning that movement around tends to lower frequency. Strong compression makes the spring-like effect important; a stronger return toward the usual spacing tends to raise frequency. The two formant directions follow from applying these same rules to the two mode patterns.

The three-times relation between the two frequencies belongs to the ideal uniform reference. **F1 and F2** identify air-column resonances, which can change when the tract shape changes. They are different from the source harmonics, whose spacing comes from vocal-fold repetition.

sections.title: Lip loading lowers both F1 and F2 in the /u/ model
teaching: The **/u/ model** places the added loading near the lip end. Both Mode 1 and Mode 2 have strong air movement there. The enlarged masses represent the greater effective mass that has to take part in this movement.

A moving mass tends to keep moving. Increasing it makes the motion harder to change and reverse. When this mass effect matters more than the stiffness effect, the vibration takes longer to complete a cycle. A longer cycle means a lower frequency.

That explanation applies to both modes at the lips. **F1 falls and F2 falls** because strong movement makes the mass effect important in both. Their shared direction comes from this location in the two patterns. It does not establish that every narrowing lowers every resonance.

The predicted directions connect the vowel shape to the air’s behavior. Lip loading changes a strongly moving region, the extra mass slows reversal, and both resonances become lower. The circles continue to move back and forth, so the enlarged elements still represent an oscillation rather than air flowing steadily out of the mouth.

sections.title: A front constriction separates the effects on F1 and F2
teaching: The **/i/ model** narrows the front region, about two thirds of the way from the glottis toward the lips. The same position is changed for both modes. The formants respond differently because the first and second modes organize their motion differently there.

In **Mode 1**, the region takes part strongly in air movement. The mass effect matters most. Increasing the effective mass makes the moving air harder to turn around, so the cycle becomes slower and **F1 falls**.

In **Mode 2**, that region takes part strongly in compression and expansion. The spring-like effect matters most. A stronger restoring response brings the air back toward its usual spacing more quickly, so the cycle becomes faster and **F2 rises**.

The opposite formant directions come from the same physical rules applied to two different patterns. Mass still tends to slow vibration, and stiffness still tends to speed it. A single narrowing produces both results because it changes a moving region in one mode and a strongly compressing region in the other.

sections.title: A back constriction reverses the F1 and F2 pattern
teaching: The **/a/ model** places the narrowing about one third of the way along the tract from the glottis. This is farther back than the front narrowing used for /i/. Both modes receive the change at the same back location, but their movement and compression patterns differ there.
In **Mode 1**, the region has strong compression changes. Strengthening the spring-like response returns the air toward its usual spacing more quickly. Vibration becomes faster, so **F1 rises**.
In **Mode 2**, the region takes part more strongly in mass movement. The added effective mass makes that movement harder to reverse. The cycle takes longer, so **F2 falls**.

The result reverses the /i/ pattern because the narrowing has moved to a different part of each mode. The mass and spring rules have stayed the same. Comparing the location with the two patterns explains why the first formant rises while the second falls, instead of treating the vowel’s arrows as unrelated facts to memorize.

sections.title: Air motion and compression in the vocal-tract modes
teaching: Air vibrates by moving back and forth while its local spacing changes. The circles move along the length of the tube, return through their usual positions, and reverse. This is **longitudinal movement**. They do not trace out the sideways shape of a vibrating string.

A group can move a long way together while the gaps between its members remain nearly constant. That emphasizes moving mass. In another region, neighbors move by different amounts, so their gaps shrink and expand. That emphasizes **compression and rarefaction**, the changes that give the air its spring-like restoring response.

The schwa row provides the moving reference, while the **F1, F2, and F3** rows separate the resonance patterns of that air column. Higher modes fit more alternations into the same tract. Their strong-motion and strong-compression regions therefore lie in different places.

Changing the air at one location can affect these modes differently. Added mass matters where substantial movement occurs. Changed stiffness matters where compression and expansion are strong. Looking at these local behaviors explains how one vocal tract can have several formants and why one narrowing can move them in different directions.

sections.title: The vocal-fold source sets harmonic spacing
teaching: The vibrating vocal folds supply the **source** for voiced speech. Their fundamental frequency, **F0**, describes how often the pattern repeats. Repetition produces harmonic components at multiples of that frequency, so F0 also sets the gap between neighboring harmonics in the source spectrum.

The examples compare a slower source with faster ones. The source rates are 100, 250, and 350 Hz. Moving from one example to the next spreads the harmonic stems farther apart. A lower rate places more harmonics inside the same frequency window, while a higher rate leaves fewer components and wider gaps.

The source descriptions connect this change to the physical system. Heavier, looser folds are associated with slower repetition in the comparison. Lighter, tighter folds are associated with faster repetition. As with the mass-and-spring explanation, the tendency to keep moving and the strength of the restoring action help determine how quickly a cycle repeats.

The membrane comparison separates several patterns and combines their movements into one surface. Its harmonic frequencies were deliberately chosen to make that combination clear. The spatial pattern describes where the membrane moves, while the frequency describes how quickly it repeats. The chosen spacing does not show that every natural membrane has harmonic resonances.

A voiced vowel contains multiple frequencies. **F0** concerns the source’s repetition and harmonic spacing. The vocal tract then makes some of those components stronger than others. Changing pitch changes the source rate; changing the vowel shape changes the tract’s favored regions. These are two different parts of how the sound is produced.

sections.title: The vocal-tract filter favors nearby harmonics
teaching: The **vocal tract** changes the balance of the harmonics supplied by the source. Some frequency regions make its air resonate strongly, so nearby harmonics become prominent. Components farther from those regions become weaker in the simplified example. This is why the tract is called a **filter**.

A **formant** is a favored resonance region of that filter. The tongue and lips reshape the air passage, which changes its resonances. The central reference, lip narrowing, front narrowing, and back/open comparison therefore produce different patterns, even though the source can supply the same harmonic spacing to each one.

The schwa example marks separated first and second resonances. The /u/ example places the first two lower and also shows a third. The front /i/ or /I/ example has a low first formant and a much higher second formant. In the /a/ example, the first two targets are close together, at 800 and 900 Hz. Those close targets describe this particular filter drawing.

A formant target and a harmonic stem have different meanings. The target describes where the tract favors sound. The stem describes a frequency actually supplied by the repeating source. A target can fall between two stems, and the nearby harmonics can still be strengthened. Filtering changes their relative strengths without requiring a new harmonic exactly at every target.

sections.title: One filter can look different at different pitches
teaching: The comparison separates changes in the **source** from changes in the **filter**. Within a column, the vowel shape stays fixed while F0 changes. Across a row, harmonic spacing stays fixed while the vowel filter changes. These two comparisons show which part of the sound changes when one part of the system is held constant.

At low F0, the harmonics are close together. Many stems fall within each broad resonance region, and their heights give a more detailed picture of its shape. At higher F0, the gaps are wider. Fewer components lie near each target, and the strongest stem can fall beside a target instead of directly on it.

The smooth **envelope** describes the pattern of strengths favored by the filter. The harmonic stems sample that pattern at the frequencies supplied by the source. A sparse set of stems leaves more of the envelope between the observed components, making the formants harder to read even when the tract shape is unchanged.

This matters especially for the two nearby /a/ targets. With few harmonics nearby, they can appear as one grouped region. More closely spaced harmonics provide more information, although they do not guarantee two separate visible peaks. Difficulty separating the peaks is different from evidence that one physical resonance has disappeared.

The stem’s horizontal position gives its frequency, and its height gives its strength after filtering. The target marks belong to the filter. When the targets stay in place but the stems spread farther apart, the source has changed how the same filter is represented. That distinction prevents a change in pitch from being mistaken for a change in vowel shape.

sections.title: Map spectra into a spectrogram
teaching: A **spectrum** describes the components present in a short slice of sound. Frequency runs horizontally, and the height of a stem shows its amplitude. The successive spectra compare three /i/ slices followed by three /a/ slices, so changes in their stronger frequency regions can be followed over time.

A **spectrogram** arranges successive slices with time running from left to right. Frequency runs upward. A component farther to the right in a spectrum appears higher in the spectrogram because both positions mean a higher frequency.

Amplitude is represented differently. A taller spectral component becomes a darker mark at its frequency and time. In this display, high amplitude is black, medium amplitude is gray, and low amplitude is white. Darkness therefore describes strength, while vertical position describes frequency.

A band moving upward is changing to a higher frequency. A band getting darker without changing height is becoming stronger at the same frequency. Keeping these two readings separate prevents a change in amplitude from being mistaken for a change in a formant’s frequency.

In the **/i/ to /a/** transition, the first strong band rises and the second falls as the resonance pattern changes. One upper band also moves downward, while a fainter band stays in the higher-frequency region. The paths connect information from adjacent time slices. They show a changing sound through time, rather than one spectrum in which the horizontal direction also means time.

sections.title: Reflection prompt
Speech-complexity experiment prompt
Use formants as input to vowel recognition
teaching: **Formants** provide useful inputs for a vowel-recognition task because they describe regions that the vocal tract makes strong. F1 and F2 give two measurements of that pattern. The network can therefore start from a compact description of the vowel’s resonances rather than from every point in the sound waveform.

The intended output answers a different kind of question. The input gives measurements of the sound, while the output distinguishes candidate vowel categories. A recognition model must learn how patterns in the measurements relate to those categories. The numbers are the evidence it receives; the category is the decision it is meant to make.

The proposed exercise is to train a network using students’ formant measurements. It connects the physical explanation of speech to an AI task. The stated plan establishes the inputs and the recognition goal, while a claim about recognition accuracy would require results from a completed test.

sections.title: A fully connected linear vowel network
teaching: The network has **two inputs**, F1 and F2. Each one has a fixed meaning, so their order matters. The network receives those measurements, passes their information through hidden layers, and produces five values associated with candidate labels.

In a **fully connected layer**, each receiving neuron gets a connection from every neuron in the preceding layer. Every connection has its own **weight**. The receiving neuron multiplies each incoming value by its weight and then adds those results. Different receiving neurons can use different weights, so they can form different combinations of the same inputs.

The first hidden layer has three neurons, the next has two, and the next has four. A hidden neuron’s value is an intermediate result used by the following layer. It is not a new formant measured from the sound, and it is not a vowel category that has already been established as correct. Each layer works with the values produced by the one before it.

The final five units correspond, from top to bottom, to /done/, /dune/, /dean/, /Don/, and /Dan/. Interpreting an output requires keeping each number attached to the correct label. Changing their order without changing the labels would change the meaning of the result.

The network is **purely linear**. There is no activation function between its layers to add another kind of transformation after a weighted sum. The layers pass their weighted results onward. That describes how information is combined, but it does not by itself make the last values into probabilities.

sections.title: Random weights assign signed contributions to connections
teaching: The input example gives **F1 as 320 and F2 as 2000**. These numbers describe the sound being presented. The connection weights play a different role: they determine how the network uses those measurements. The same example can produce different internal results when it passes through different weights.

Each connection supplies one **weight** for one incoming value. A neuron multiplies the incoming values by their respective weights and adds the products. A neuron receiving the two formant inputs therefore has two incoming weights. The three neurons in the first hidden layer can combine that same input pair in three different ways.

A weight’s sign controls the direction of its contribution for a given input, while its size controls how strongly that connection contributes. Some contributions can reinforce one another, and others can oppose one another when added. The final sum depends on the collection of incoming contributions, rather than on a single connection considered alone.

The weights shown are random starting values. They describe how the untrained network is initially connected, rather than knowledge it has already learned about vowels. A label attached to an output gives that output its intended meaning; it does not prove that the current random weights recognize that label correctly.

A **forward pass** uses the current measurements and weights to produce an output. **Learning** would change the weights so that the network’s combinations become more useful for the task. Keeping inputs and weights separate makes the difference clear: the input is the example being processed, while the weights are the settings used to process examples.

sections.title: Forward flow and an illustrative output distribution
teaching: A **forward pass** carries the formant information through the network with the weights it currently has. The first layer combines F1 and F2, the next combines those results, and the later layers continue the process. Producing an output with the current settings is different from learning, which changes the weights.

The illustrated output gives /done/ a value of 0.5, /Dan/ a value of 0.2, and each other candidate a value of 0.1. The largest value means the model favors /done/ in that illustration. The smaller values leave support for alternatives rather than saying that each other candidate is impossible.

A **probability distribution** across these candidates uses values between zero and one that add to one. The illustrated bars satisfy those conditions. The purely linear code does not include the step that would ensure such a distribution, so the bars illustrate an intended output rather than a verified calculation from the displayed weights.

The **predicted category** is the one the model favors. The **true category** is the category the example actually belongs to. Those are different pieces of information. To decide whether the prediction is right, the true category must be supplied; the reaction symbol alone does not identify it.

sections.title: Declare the layer sequence in PyTorch
teaching: The code defines the drawn network in **PyTorch**. Importing torch makes the library available. Importing torch.nn as nn provides a short name for its neural-network building blocks. The variable net is assigned the model assembled from those blocks.

**nn.Sequential** places layers in the order their results will pass through. Each **nn.Linear** layer takes incoming values and produces outgoing weighted sums. The first argument gives how many inputs it receives, and the second gives how many outputs it produces. In nn.Linear(2, 3, bias=False), two incoming measurements are combined separately by three receiving neurons.

The following layers take three values and produce two, then take two and produce four, then take four and produce five. Each stage is connected to the next because the number it produces matches the number the next one expects. The five final values belong to the five candidate labels in the diagram.

Every receiving unit has one weight for each incoming value. The code’s **bias=False** removes an extra constant that would otherwise be added to its weighted sum. It does not remove those weights or stop them from changing during learning. With no activation-function layers between the Linear calls, the sequence stays purely linear.

Defining this sequence establishes the model’s structure. Passing a formant example into it would use that structure to produce an output. Training would additionally require examples and a process for changing the weights. The supplied code is a declaration, so it does not itself demonstrate training or compute the illustrated probability distribution.

lecture15.title: Neural Networks · Forward propagation, learning, and sigmoid

sections.title: Neural Networks
Two formants feed a fully connected network
teaching: **F1 and F2** are the two formant measurements supplied to the network. The five output positions stand for **done, dune, dean, Don, and Dan**, in that order. The network receives measurements of the sound and produces a response for each possible word. The input positions and output positions therefore have different jobs, even though both are drawn as circles. Between the inputs and outputs are three **hidden layers**, containing three, two, and four neurons. A hidden neuron receives values from the layer before it and sends its result onward. The arrangement is **2 → 3 → 2 → 4 → 5**. These numbers count the units in successive layers. They do not count recordings or training trials.

**Fully connected** means that every neuron in one layer connects to every neuron in the next layer. Each connection has its own **weight**, which controls how the value traveling along that connection contributes to the receiving neuron. A positive weight preserves the sign of its contribution, while a negative weight reverses it. The receiving neuron combines all its incoming contributions.

The same input can affect several hidden neurons because its outgoing connections carry different weights. F1 contributes to all three neurons in the first hidden layer, but it is not multiplied by the same number on every connection. F2 also reaches those three neurons. Each neuron therefore combines the same two measurements in its own way.

The weights are fixed for this network description. Changing a formant measurement changes what travels through the connections. Changing a weight changes how strongly a connection contributes. Those are different changes to the system. A connection weight specifies how a value contributes to a receiving neuron, rather than giving the probability of an individual word.

sections.title: Forward propagation combines weighted inputs
teaching: **Forward propagation** carries information from the inputs through the hidden layers to the outputs. F1 is **320** and F2 is **2000**. For the top neuron in the first hidden layer, each input is multiplied by its connection weight, and the two products are added. The positive contribution from F1 and the negative contribution from F2 combine to give **−0.40**. This multiplication followed by addition is an **inner product**. The other two neurons receive the same formants through different weights, so their results are **6.64** and **2.72**. A negative result is still a value that the next layer can use. It does not mean that the neuron or its connections have disappeared.

Each later layer repeats the same operation using the values from the layer immediately before it. The next pair is approximately **5.50 and −5.93**. Those two values then produce four hidden values, approximately **1.57, −1.95, −1.95, and −2.88**. Information moves through the layers in that order because a later neuron requires the earlier neurons’ results.

The five final weighted sums are **logits**, or scores before they become probabilities. **Softmax** exponentiates each score and divides it by the sum of the exponentiated scores. The resulting probabilities share one total. A negative logit can therefore lead to a positive probability, and a positive hidden value is not itself a probability.

**Done** receives the largest probability, about **55.7%**, while **dean** receives about **8.1%**. These are the network’s current responses to this input. They do not establish the true word. The hidden activations here are linear, the weights stay fixed during the forward pass, and the calculations retain more precision than the rounded labels.

sections.title: Pop quiz · Forward propagation
Info on Exam 2 and Exam 3
Backpropagation uses the difference between prediction and target
teaching: The **computed output** is the network’s current probability distribution. The **desired output** identifies **dean** with a 1 and gives the other four words a 0. This target says which word belongs to the recording. It does not describe the probabilities the untrained network already produces, so the largest computed response can disagree with the desired word. **Cross-entropy loss** measures the mismatch using the probability assigned to the true word. Dean currently receives only about **8.1%**. Assigning more probability to dean reduces this loss, while assigning it less increases the loss. The target and computed output therefore supply the information needed to evaluate how the weights contribute to the mistake.

**Backpropagation** works backward from the output connections toward the input connections. The final layer’s contribution to the loss is found first. That information is then used to determine how the preceding hidden layers contributed. The calculation proceeds from the output connections to the connections into hidden layer 3, hidden layer 2, and finally hidden layer 1.

A **gradient** describes how the loss changes with a small change in a weight. The update subtracts the learning rate times that gradient from the old weight. A positive gradient leads to a decrease in that weight, and a negative gradient leads to an increase. Learning therefore does not mean making every positive connection larger or every negative connection smaller.

The activations and probabilities stored from the forward pass stay fixed throughout the backward calculation. All gradients use the original weights and stored activations, so they belong to one simultaneous parameter update. A new forward pass would be required to obtain the updated network’s predictions. The input connections use a smaller learning rate because their inputs are raw formant values in hertz.

sections.title: Predict how changing a marked weight affects error
teaching: Increasing a weight changes its contribution to the receiving neuron, but its effect on **error** depends on what that contribution eventually does to the outputs. The desired word is **dean**, while the network currently gives its largest probability to **done**. The relevant question is how a small weight change affects the probability assigned to the true word. The pink-marked positive connection runs from the top neuron in the last hidden layer to **done**. That hidden neuron has a positive activation, approximately **1.57**. Increasing this weight raises done’s final score. Because softmax makes the five output probabilities share one total, strengthening this incorrect candidate reduces the probability available to dean and increases the cross-entropy loss.

The blue-marked first connection runs from **F1** to the top neuron in the first hidden layer. Increasing that weight raises the first hidden neuron’s value because F1 is positive. Its influence then passes through several positive and negative connections and reaches several outputs. The effect on the final error cannot be decided from the sign of this first connection alone.

For the supplied network and dean target, the full backward calculation gives a positive gradient for this input connection too. A small increase therefore raises the error here, while the update decreases the weight. The two marked connections both call for decreases in this example, but the early connection requires the combined influence of the downstream paths to establish that direction.

sections.title: Backpropagation reuses downstream error calculations
teaching: The **last weights**, labeled **W5**, directly determine the final output scores from the last hidden activations. Their effects on the error are close to the output comparison. Once the computed and desired outputs are available, the contribution of these final connections can be found without tracing another hidden layer beyond them. The **first weights**, labeled **W2**, affect the first hidden activations. Those activations affect two more hidden layers before the output scores are produced. An early weight’s contribution to error therefore includes what the later weights do with the values it changes. Its effect is distributed across the paths that continue from it.

**Backpropagation** calculates the effects near the output first and reuses them when working toward earlier layers. The downstream part of an early connection’s effect has already been computed. It can be combined with the local connection information instead of repeatedly solving the entire downstream calculation separately for every early weight.

This reuse is the connection to **Bellman–Viterbi dynamic programming**. Smaller dependent calculations are solved and their results are retained for the calculations that depend on them. Working backward fits the dependence of the error on the layers, because the effect of an early layer includes the layers after it.

**SGD** supplies the weight-adjustment rule, while backpropagation efficiently supplies the gradients that rule uses. Combining **SGD with dynamic programming** connects these two jobs. The backward calculation determines how the error depends on the weights, and the optimizer uses those results to change the weights.

sections.title: Pair each recording with its target row
teaching: The **Formant_Inputs** matrix has **110 rows and two columns**. Each row contains F1 and F2 for one recording, so the columns represent the two sound measurements rather than two possible words. The network processes the two values from a row together as one example. The **TrueVowel_Outputs** matrix has **110 rows and five columns**. Its columns are **done, dune, dean, Don, and Dan**. The row for a recording puts a 1 in the correct word’s position and 0 in the other four positions. This is a **one-hot target**, because one position identifies the category.

The rows in the two matrices must stay matched. The third input row contains **320 and 2000**, and the third target row identifies **dean**. Moving one input row without moving its matching target would pair the sound measurements with the wrong answer. Keeping the same number of rows is not sufficient if their order no longer agrees.

The complete matrices contain 110 examples in paired rows. The five listed examples identify the column arrangement rather than supplying all 110 recordings. The five target columns describe the available categories. They do not mean that each recording supplies five separate input examples.

The network’s current output is distinct from this target matrix. It assigns its own probabilities to the five words, with done currently highest for the dean example. The target records the correct label even when the network makes a mistake. Training compares those two kinds of information rather than replacing the target with the network’s strongest response.

sections.title: Read one full-batch training step in PyTorch
teaching: **X** contains the two formant values for each of the 110 recordings, and **Y** contains the five-position targets for the same recordings. **torch.load** loads the saved tensor files, and **.float()** supplies floating-point values. The program assumes these files already exist with the stated shapes. It does not create the recordings or their labels. **nn.Sequential** connects the layers in their written order. **nn.Linear(2, 3)** maps each pair of inputs into three values. The later layers map three to two, two to four, and four to five. These dimensions preserve the **2 → 3 → 2 → 4 → 5** arrangement. There is no sigmoid declared between these hidden layers.

**SGD** is given the network’s parameters and a **learning rate of 0.1**. **zero_grad()** clears previously stored gradients. **net(X)** performs the forward calculation, and **CrossEntropyLoss** compares the final scores with Y. This loss handles the softmax-related calculation internally, so the final linear layer supplies logits rather than a separately declared softmax output.

**loss.backward()** computes the gradients of the loss with respect to the parameters. **sgd.step()** then changes those parameters using the gradients. These are separate operations. Computing how a weight affects the error does not by itself change that weight, and clearing gradients does not erase the learned parameter values.

All **110 rows** contribute to this one gradient step. The code has no repeated training loop. It also uses PyTorch’s default linear-layer initialization and bias options, whereas the numerical drawing uses hand-selected weights with no biases. The code specifies the same layer sizes, but it does not automatically reproduce the displayed numbers.

sections.title: Sigmoid turns an inner product into a bounded activation
teaching: The **sigmoid activation function** takes an inner product as its input and returns a value between 0 and 1. A large negative input produces an activation near 0, and a large positive input produces one near 1. The S-shaped relationship is gradual rather than an exact switch that returns only two possible values. The horizontal coordinate is **linear activation**, the weighted sum before sigmoid, and the vertical coordinate is **sigmoid activation**. An input of **−4** gives about **0.0180**, whereas an input of **4** gives about **0.9820**. Around the center the curve is steep. Near the upper and lower ends it flattens, so further input changes produce relatively small output changes.

The formula divides 1 by 1 plus the exponential of the negative input. Moving the input toward larger positive values makes that denominator approach 1, so the output approaches 1. Moving it toward larger negative values enlarges the denominator, so the output approaches 0. The weighted sum is transformed rather than simply passed on unchanged.

Physical differences can be compressed or emphasized by this input–activation relationship. Distinct inputs near a flat end give similar activations, while inputs on different sides of the steep central region can produce much more different activations. Similarity in the incoming measurements therefore does not translate into an equal-sized difference at every point in the response.

**Edgar Adrian** supplies biological context through work on nerve activity, including the 1932 Nobel Prize. The mathematical sigmoid is a model of graded activation. Adrian’s rate-coding work concerns changes in firing rate, so a bounded model activation should not be confused with the claim that biological neurons can only have two possible firing rates.

sections.title: Apply sigmoid while recalculating downstream activity
teaching: The inputs remain **F1 = 320** and **F2 = 2000**, and the connection weights stay fixed. Sigmoid is added to the **nine hidden neurons**, one neuron at a time, in the order of three neurons in the first hidden layer, two in the second, and four in the third. Purple neurons remain linear, while green neurons pass their inner product through sigmoid. The first hidden neuron changes from **−0.400** to about **0.401**. Its new output changes what the next layer receives, so all downstream values are recalculated. The process is not a matter of putting sigmoid around every number stored from the all-linear network. Once an earlier output changes, the later weighted sums change as well.

After all three first-layer neurons use sigmoid, their outputs are approximately **0.401, 0.999, and 0.938**. Applying sigmoid to the recalculated second-layer sums gives about **0.713 and 0.223**. These second-layer values then supply the third layer, whose final sigmoid outputs are about **0.599, 0.609, 0.609, and 0.481**.

The output layer still uses **softmax** to assign probabilities across the five words. Once all hidden neurons use sigmoid, **Dan** has the largest displayed probability, about **32.0%**, and **dean** has about **23.0%**. The relative output pattern changes even though the inputs and connection weights have not changed.

This sequence changes the hidden activation rule rather than training the weights. Dean’s probability is higher than in the all-linear starting state, but it is still not the largest response. Adding sigmoid can therefore alter which word the network favors without establishing that the network has learned the correct classification.

sections.title: Insert sigmoid after the hidden linear layers
teaching: The network still receives **two formant measurements** and produces **five output scores**. Its linear layers keep the dimensions **2 → 3 → 2 → 4 → 5**. The change is that **nn.Sigmoid()** follows each of the first three linear layers. Each hidden layer therefore combines its incoming values and then transforms those sums before passing them onward. Sigmoid changes values without changing how many values a layer produces. The three values from the first linear layer remain three values after sigmoid, which is why the following **nn.Linear(3, 2)** still receives the correct input size. The same relationship holds for the two-value and four-value hidden layers.

The final **nn.Linear(4, 5)** is not followed by a declared sigmoid. Its five scores go to **CrossEntropyLoss**, which performs the softmax-related loss calculation internally. Hidden sigmoid activations and the final class-probability calculation have different roles. Adding a hidden activation does not turn every hidden neuron into one of the five word categories.

The training sequence remains **zero_grad**, the forward calculation and loss, **backward**, and **step**. Clearing gradients prepares this step, the loss compares predictions with the paired targets, backpropagation computes parameter gradients, and SGD applies the update. The learning rate remains **0.1**, and all 110 recordings contribute to the one displayed step.

The numerical drawing uses the original illustrative weights and no biases, with sigmoid added to the hidden neurons. The short PyTorch declaration initializes its own parameters with the default options. Its structure matches the hidden-activation change, but reproducing the particular displayed probabilities would also require the matching parameter values and bias choices.
